title: WHAT IF YOU LIVED ON MARS FOR A YEAR?

segments.line: Four people just spent 378 days
sealed inside a fake Mars.
No windows.
No live calls home.
Every message takes up to twenty-two minutes each way.
Here's what a year
like that does to you.
Day one. The hatch seals behind you.
A calendar on the wall starts counting,
and it won't stop
for a very long time.
What if you lived on Mars for a year?
First, the address.
It's a 3D-printed habitat
at NASA's Johnson Space Center, in Houston.
Its name is Mars Dune Alpha.
Roughly seventeen hundred square feet,
with every wall printed layer by layer.
That's a small house with no front door.
Four volunteers walked in
on the nineteenth of October, twenty twenty-five.
Ross Elder, the commander and a test pilot.
Ellen Ellis, the medical officer.
James Spicer, the flight engineer.
And Matthew Montgomery, the science officer.
You're along for the ride,
in a very small orange jumpsuit.
Time for a quick tour.
Kitchen, bunks, garden, gym.
Spot what's missing from the floor plan.
Windows. Zero of them.
Which makes the phone situation interesting.
No windows means no sunrise.
No weather check.
No peeking at the street.
No outside sounds either.
No traffic, no birds.
And no real-time calls with family and friends.
A message from here takes
up to twenty-two minutes each way.
So you text your mum: how's the dog?
Then you wait.
You make a snack.
You wait some more.
You rearrange the spice jars. Still waiting.
By the time her answer lands,
you've thought of a few more questions.
You send them all. Now she waits.
It's less a conversation,
more a very slow postcard.
But waiting isn't the hardest part of the day.
Next up: stepping outside. Sort of.
Every so often,
the crew heads out for a Marswalk.
It's simulated, but the suits are very real work.
First, you get suited up.
Preparing the suits takes time.
Then come the airlock steps,
one careful move after another.
Then long traverses across the sandy terrain.
Elder said all of it took time and stamina.
So the crew looked after the basics.
Good nutrition. Regular exercise. Proper rest.
Stamina is something you build,
not something you wish for.
You trudge through the sand. Slowly. Bravely.
Your legs would like a word with management.
Walking on Mars is mostly walking.
Good thing not every job needs legs.
Some of the exploring never leaves the building.
From inside, the crew remotely flew a drone,
and drove a rover.
Both went out to survey the terrain.
They hunted for rocks
worth identifying, or collecting.
You grip the controller. Your tongue sticks out.
Elder, the test pilot,
called flying the drone "uncannily similar" to flying.
Your rover rolls forward. Then turns left. Slowly.
Like a very polite shopping cart.
It scoops up a rock. You name it Kevin.
But every robot trip
needs a base that doesn't break.
And somebody has to keep the base running.
That somebody is James Spicer, the flight engineer.
His job: keep the systems running.
The crew also tracked their consumables.
That's everything you use up,
from dish soap to respirator filters.
Everyone was careful with food and water.
Spicer compared it
to living on a submarine, or a boat.
So you count the dish soap like it's treasure.
You tick the clipboard.
Then you tick it again.
Pip's rule: whoever finishes the soap, announces it.
Speaking of things you can't run out of, food.
Luckily, you grow some.
Welcome to the garden.
Montgomery, the science officer, works the crops.
They grew hydroponic vegetables.
That's plants with roots in water, not soil.
Pink lights. Tidy pipes. Leafy green hopes.
There was also a seed-germination experiment.
Seeds in simulated Martian soil,
next to a control.
A control is just ordinary soil,
so you can compare.
You water both rows.
You whisper encouragement to one.
That's not in the protocol.
Harvest day arrives. Everyone gathers round.
Your vegetable is, let's say, compact.
You divide it into four portions.
Equal. Very scientific.
What sprouts best
is exactly what the data is for.
Gardening is a workout,
but it's not the whole workout.
Staying healthy is a daily job.
There's a stationary bike in the habitat.
You pedal hard and arrive absolutely nowhere.
Very Mars.
Ellen Ellis, the medical officer,
looks after the crew's health.
She organised biological sample collections
for health research.
That means tubes and labels,
and a very patient medical officer.
Every sample helps researchers understand a year inside.
You roll up a sleeve. You smile bravely.
Your body is covered.
Your head is the open question.
A year with no windows. How's your head?
No constant news. No endless scrolling.
Spicer was surprised by how little he missed it.
News and social media, gone, and life went on.
What filled the gap?
Stories and jokes around the kitchen table.
Somebody tells the same joke again.
You laugh anyway.
Ellis said most days she didn't feel isolated.
She had three teammates to rely on.
Four people. One table.
One very long conversation.
You check the wall calendar. Still counting.
Meanwhile, the world outside kept right on moving.
And what a world it was.
While the crew stayed inside,
astronaut Jack Hathaway was in orbit.
He completed a 237-day mission on the space station.
At the same time,
the Artemis II astronauts flew around the Moon.
They set the record
for the farthest humans have travelled from Earth.
That's according to NASA.
Picture it as a split screen.
On the left, a tiny habitat in Houston.
On the right, a trip around the Moon.
The farthest you've travelled this week is the garden.
And back at the habitat,
the calendar is nearly full.
Then, finally, the last morning.
On the thirty-first of October, twenty twenty-six,
the crew stepped out.
Three hundred seventy-eight days,
and this was their first time outdoors.
Family and friends were there to welcome them.
The calendar hits day three hundred seventy-eight.
Pip squints at the sun.
It's very bright. It's very sun.
There's wind. Actual wind.
You even hear a distant lawnmower. Beautiful.
Then come the hugs.
A year of waiting, and no delay at all.
But why live in a fake Mars in the first place?
Because the real Mars is far,
and real crews will need answers first.
Everything the crew did becomes data.
Data for future Mars crews.
And for NASA's Moon Base planning, too.
Sara Whiting calls this "the now moment."
The first mission like this ended
on the sixth of July, twenty twenty-four.
Now a second crew has added their 378 days.
Could you last a year?
Tell us what you'd miss first.
Tomorrow: a new what if.
